title: Daily orders with a 7-day moving average
q: For December 2024, show every OrderDate with Orders, Revenue (sum of OrderTotal), Avg7Day (average daily orders over that day and the 6 days before it, 1 decimal) and VsAvgPct (Orders compared with Avg7Day, as a percentage above or below, 1 decimal). The first days of December must still average over late-November days. Sort by OrderDate.
sql:
WITH d AS (
    SELECT OrderDate, COUNT(*) AS Orders, SUM(OrderTotal) AS Revenue
    FROM ecommerce.Orders
    GROUP BY OrderDate
), w AS (
    SELECT OrderDate, Orders, Revenue,
           AVG(CAST(Orders AS decimal(9,2))) OVER (ORDER BY OrderDate ROWS BETWEEN 6 PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW) AS A7
    FROM d
)
SELECT OrderDate, Orders, Revenue, CAST(A7 AS decimal(9,1)) AS Avg7Day,
       CAST(100.0 * (Orders - A7) / A7 AS decimal(9,1)) AS VsAvgPct
FROM w
WHERE OrderDate >= '2024-12-01' AND OrderDate < '2025-01-01'
ORDER BY OrderDate;
how: Aggregate to one row per day, compute the moving average with ROWS BETWEEN 6 PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW over *all* days, and filter to December only in the outer query. Filtering first would cut the November days out of the window.
a:
**Approach hint:** Aggregate to one row per day, compute the moving average with ROWS BETWEEN 6 PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW over *all* days, and filter to December only in the outer query. Filtering first would cut the November days out of the window.

title: Busiest hour of each weekday
q: Using PlacedAt, count orders per weekday and hour of the day (0-23). For each weekday show the busiest hour: Weekday (Monday, Tuesday, ...), HourOfDay, Orders and ShareOfDayPct (that hour's share of the weekday's orders, 2 decimals). Keep ties. Sort Monday to Sunday, then HourOfDay.
sql:
WITH h AS (
    SELECT DATEDIFF(day, '19000101', PlacedAt) % 7 AS DayNo,
           DATENAME(weekday, PlacedAt) AS Weekday,
           DATEPART(hour, PlacedAt) AS HourOfDay,
           COUNT(*) AS Orders
    FROM ecommerce.Orders
    GROUP BY DATEDIFF(day, '19000101', PlacedAt) % 7, DATENAME(weekday, PlacedAt), DATEPART(hour, PlacedAt)
), r AS (
    SELECT *, RANK() OVER (PARTITION BY DayNo ORDER BY Orders DESC) AS rk,
           SUM(Orders) OVER (PARTITION BY DayNo) AS DayOrders
    FROM h
)
SELECT Weekday, HourOfDay, Orders, CAST(100.0 * Orders / DayOrders AS decimal(5,2)) AS ShareOfDayPct
FROM r
WHERE rk = 1
ORDER BY DayNo, HourOfDay;
how: 1900-01-01 was a Monday, so DATEDIFF(day, '19000101', d) % 7 numbers Monday as 0 whatever the server's DATEFIRST setting. RANK() per weekday keeps tied hours; a window SUM over the same partition gives the day total for the share.
a:
**Approach hint:** 1900-01-01 was a Monday, so DATEDIFF(day, '19000101', d) % 7 numbers Monday as 0 whatever the server's DATEFIRST setting. RANK() per weekday keeps tied hours; a window SUM over the same partition gives the day total for the share.

title: Same-day power buyers
q: Find customers who placed 3 or more orders on the same day. Show CustomerID, CustomerName, OrderDate, OrdersThatDay, DaySpend (sum of OrderTotal that day), FirstAt and LastAt (time of their first and last order that day) and MinutesBetween (from first to last). Sort by OrdersThatDay descending, then DaySpend descending, then CustomerID, OrderDate.
sql:
SELECT o.CustomerID, c.CustomerName, o.OrderDate, COUNT(*) AS OrdersThatDay, SUM(o.OrderTotal) AS DaySpend,
       MIN(o.PlacedAt) AS FirstAt, MAX(o.PlacedAt) AS LastAt,
       DATEDIFF(minute, MIN(o.PlacedAt), MAX(o.PlacedAt)) AS MinutesBetween
FROM ecommerce.Orders AS o
JOIN ecommerce.Customers AS c ON c.CustomerID = o.CustomerID
GROUP BY o.CustomerID, c.CustomerName, o.OrderDate
HAVING COUNT(*) >= 3
ORDER BY OrdersThatDay DESC, DaySpend DESC, o.CustomerID, o.OrderDate;
how: Group by customer *and* day, then HAVING COUNT(*) >= 3. MIN and MAX of the timestamp in the same group give the first and last order.
a:

title: Bazaar Days lift
q: Everyday Bazaar ran its Bazaar Days sale on 16 and 17 July 2024. For each sale day show SaleDay, Orders, BaselineOrders (average orders on the same weekday in the 4 weeks before), OrderLiftPct, Revenue, BaselineRevenue and RevenueLiftPct (lift = (sale − baseline) ÷ baseline × 100). Round baselines and percentages to 1 decimal. Sort by SaleDay.
sql:
WITH d AS (
    SELECT OrderDate, COUNT(*) AS Orders, SUM(OrderTotal) AS Revenue
    FROM ecommerce.Orders
    GROUP BY OrderDate
), b AS (
    SELECT s.OrderDate AS SaleDay, s.Orders, s.Revenue,
           AVG(CAST(p.Orders AS decimal(12,2))) AS BaseOrders, AVG(p.Revenue) AS BaseRevenue
    FROM d AS s
    JOIN d AS p ON p.OrderDate IN (DATEADD(day, -7, s.OrderDate), DATEADD(day, -14, s.OrderDate),
                                   DATEADD(day, -21, s.OrderDate), DATEADD(day, -28, s.OrderDate))
    WHERE s.OrderDate IN ('2024-07-16', '2024-07-17')
    GROUP BY s.OrderDate, s.Orders, s.Revenue
)
SELECT SaleDay, Orders, CAST(BaseOrders AS decimal(9,1)) AS BaselineOrders,
       CAST(100.0 * (Orders - BaseOrders) / BaseOrders AS decimal(9,1)) AS OrderLiftPct,
       Revenue, CAST(BaseRevenue AS decimal(12,1)) AS BaselineRevenue,
       CAST(100.0 * (Revenue - BaseRevenue) / BaseRevenue AS decimal(9,1)) AS RevenueLiftPct
FROM b
ORDER BY SaleDay;
how: Build a daily table once, then self-join it: each sale day joins to the four days exactly 7, 14, 21 and 28 days earlier (same weekday). Comparing with the same weekday matters because weekends are busier.
a:
**Approach hint:** Build a daily table once, then self-join it: each sale day joins to the four days exactly 7, 14, 21 and 28 days earlier (same weekday). Comparing with the same weekday matters because weekends are busier.

title: Settlement check by order status
q: Total each order's payments (an order can have a gift card plus a card). For each OrderStatus show Orders, FullyPaid (payments equal OrderTotal), Unpaid (no payment), PartPaid (some, but less), Overpaid, and OutstandingAmount (OrderTotal minus payments, over all orders of that status). Sort by OrderStatus.
sql:
WITH p AS (
    SELECT OrderID, SUM(PaidAmount) AS Paid
    FROM ecommerce.Payments
    GROUP BY OrderID
)
SELECT o.OrderStatus, COUNT(*) AS Orders,
       SUM(CASE WHEN p.Paid = o.OrderTotal THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) AS FullyPaid,
       SUM(CASE WHEN p.Paid IS NULL THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) AS Unpaid,
       SUM(CASE WHEN p.Paid < o.OrderTotal THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) AS PartPaid,
       SUM(CASE WHEN p.Paid > o.OrderTotal THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) AS Overpaid,
       SUM(o.OrderTotal - COALESCE(p.Paid, 0)) AS OutstandingAmount
FROM ecommerce.Orders AS o
LEFT JOIN p ON p.OrderID = o.OrderID
GROUP BY o.OrderStatus
ORDER BY o.OrderStatus;
how: Sum payments per order in a CTE *before* joining, or a split payment would count the order twice. LEFT JOIN keeps unpaid orders; their Paid is NULL, which matches none of the comparisons and needs its own IS NULL test.
a:
**Approach hint:** Sum payments per order in a CTE *before* joining, or a split payment would count the order twice. LEFT JOIN keeps unpaid orders; their Paid is NULL, which matches none of the comparisons and needs its own IS NULL test.

title: Fan-out trap: one report, three totals
q: For each SalesChannel show Orders, Revenue (sum of OrderTotal), ItemsSold (sum of OrderItems.Quantity) and Paid (sum of Payments.PaidAmount). Every number must be right. Sort by Revenue descending.
sql:
WITH i AS (
    SELECT OrderID, SUM(Quantity) AS Qty FROM ecommerce.OrderItems GROUP BY OrderID
), p AS (
    SELECT OrderID, SUM(PaidAmount) AS Paid FROM ecommerce.Payments GROUP BY OrderID
)
SELECT o.SalesChannel, COUNT(*) AS Orders, SUM(o.OrderTotal) AS Revenue,
       SUM(COALESCE(i.Qty, 0)) AS ItemsSold, SUM(COALESCE(p.Paid, 0)) AS Paid
FROM ecommerce.Orders AS o
LEFT JOIN i ON i.OrderID = o.OrderID
LEFT JOIN p ON p.OrderID = o.OrderID
GROUP BY o.SalesChannel
ORDER BY Revenue DESC;
how: Joining Orders to OrderItems and Payments in one go repeats each order once per item *and* per payment, which inflates Revenue and Paid. Pre-aggregate each child table to one row per order, then join.

title: First-month cohort retention
q: Group customers by the month of their first order. For each first month show FirstMonth (yyyy-MM), NewCustomers (how many customers started that month), ReturnedWithin30 (how many had another order on a later date within 30 days of their first one) and RetentionPct (2 decimals). Sort by FirstMonth.
sql:
WITH e AS (
    SELECT CustomerID, OrderDate, MIN(OrderDate) OVER (PARTITION BY CustomerID) AS FirstDate
    FROM ecommerce.Orders
), c AS (
    SELECT CustomerID, FirstDate,
           MAX(CASE WHEN OrderDate > FirstDate AND OrderDate <= DATEADD(day, 30, FirstDate) THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) AS Returned
    FROM e
    GROUP BY CustomerID, FirstDate
)
SELECT FORMAT(FirstDate, 'yyyy-MM') AS FirstMonth,
       COUNT(*) AS NewCustomers,
       SUM(Returned) AS ReturnedWithin30,
       CAST(100.0 * SUM(Returned) / COUNT(*) AS decimal(5,2)) AS RetentionPct
FROM c
GROUP BY FORMAT(FirstDate, 'yyyy-MM')
ORDER BY FirstMonth;
how: Step 1: MIN(date) OVER (PARTITION BY CustomerID) tags every row with that customer's first date. Step 2: one row per customer with a 1/0 flag (MAX of a CASE). Step 3: group by the first month.
a:
**Approach hint:** Step 1: MIN(date) OVER (PARTITION BY CustomerID) tags every row with that customer's first date. Step 2: one row per customer with a 1/0 flag (MAX of a CASE). Step 3: group by the first month.

title: Top 3 sellers per department and their share
q: Rank sellers inside their Department by revenue (sum of OrderTotal on their orders). For the top 3 in each department show Department, SellerRank, SellerName, Orders, Revenue and DeptSharePct (the seller's share of the whole department's revenue, 2 decimals). Ties share a rank without skipping. Sort by Department, SellerRank, SellerName.
sql:
WITH s AS (
    SELECT se.Department, se.SellerID, se.SellerName, COUNT(*) AS Orders, SUM(o.OrderTotal) AS Revenue
    FROM ecommerce.Orders AS o
    JOIN ecommerce.Sellers AS se ON se.SellerID = o.SellerID
    GROUP BY se.Department, se.SellerID, se.SellerName
), r AS (
    SELECT *, DENSE_RANK() OVER (PARTITION BY Department ORDER BY Revenue DESC) AS SellerRank,
           SUM(Revenue) OVER (PARTITION BY Department) AS DeptRevenue
    FROM s
)
SELECT Department, SellerRank, SellerName, Orders, Revenue,
       CAST(100.0 * Revenue / DeptRevenue AS decimal(5,2)) AS DeptSharePct
FROM r
WHERE SellerRank <= 3
ORDER BY Department, SellerRank, SellerName;
how: Aggregate per seller, then two window functions over the same department partition: DENSE_RANK for the position and SUM for the department total. The share must use the total of *all* sellers, so compute it before filtering to the top 3.
a:
**Approach hint:** Aggregate per seller, then two window functions over the same department partition: DENSE_RANK for the position and SUM for the department total. The share must use the total of *all* sellers, so compute it before filtering to the top 3.

title: Bought together most often
q: Find pairs of different products that appear in the same order. Show the 10 pairs bought together most often (keep ties at 10th place): ProductA and ProductB (names; ProductA has the smaller ProductID) and TimesTogether. Sort by TimesTogether descending, then ProductA, then ProductB.
sql:
SELECT TOP (10) WITH TIES pa.ProductName AS ProductA, pb.ProductName AS ProductB, COUNT(*) AS TimesTogether
FROM ecommerce.OrderItems AS a
JOIN ecommerce.OrderItems AS b ON b.OrderID = a.OrderID AND b.ProductID > a.ProductID
JOIN ecommerce.Products AS pa ON pa.ProductID = a.ProductID
JOIN ecommerce.Products AS pb ON pb.ProductID = b.ProductID
GROUP BY a.ProductID, b.ProductID, pa.ProductName, pb.ProductName
ORDER BY TimesTogether DESC, ProductA, ProductB;
how: Self-join OrderItems on the same OrderID; b.ProductID > a.ProductID removes self-pairs and keeps each pair once. TOP (10) WITH TIES needs an ORDER BY and keeps every row tied with the 10th; the extra name columns only break display order.
a:
**Approach hint:** Self-join OrderItems on the same OrderID; b.ProductID > a.ProductID removes self-pairs and keeps each pair once. TOP (10) WITH TIES needs an ORDER BY and keeps every row tied with the 10th; the extra name columns only break display order.

title: How often do regulars come back?
q: For customers with at least 25 orders, measure the days between each order and their previous one. Per customer Region show Regulars (how many such customers), Gaps (how many gaps measured), AvgGapDays and MedianGapDays (1 decimal). Sort by MedianGapDays, then Region.
sql:
WITH r AS (
    SELECT CustomerID
    FROM ecommerce.Orders
    GROUP BY CustomerID
    HAVING COUNT(*) >= 25
), gaps AS (
    SELECT c.Region, o.CustomerID,
           DATEDIFF(day, LAG(o.OrderDate) OVER (PARTITION BY o.CustomerID ORDER BY o.PlacedAt, o.OrderID), o.OrderDate) AS GapDays
    FROM ecommerce.Orders AS o
    JOIN r ON r.CustomerID = o.CustomerID
    JOIN ecommerce.Customers AS c ON c.CustomerID = o.CustomerID
), m AS (
    SELECT Region, CustomerID, GapDays,
           PERCENTILE_CONT(0.5) WITHIN GROUP (ORDER BY GapDays) OVER (PARTITION BY Region) AS MedG
    FROM gaps
)
SELECT Region, COUNT(DISTINCT CustomerID) AS Regulars, COUNT(GapDays) AS Gaps,
       CAST(AVG(CAST(GapDays AS decimal(9,2))) AS decimal(9,1)) AS AvgGapDays,
       CAST(MAX(MedG) AS decimal(9,1)) AS MedianGapDays
FROM m
GROUP BY Region
ORDER BY MedianGapDays, Region;
how: Three steps: pick the regulars with HAVING, measure gaps with LAG per customer (the first order has no gap, so LAG returns NULL), then summarise per region. PERCENTILE_CONT exists only as a window function, so tag each row with its region's median, then GROUP BY (COUNT(DISTINCT ...) is not allowed with OVER). PERCENTILE_CONT, COUNT(column) and AVG all skip NULL gaps.
a:
**Approach hint:** Three steps: pick the regulars with HAVING, measure gaps with LAG per customer (the first order has no gap, so LAG returns NULL), then summarise per region. PERCENTILE_CONT exists only as a window function, so tag each row with its region's median, then GROUP BY (COUNT(DISTINCT ...) is not allowed with OVER). PERCENTILE_CONT, COUNT(column) and AVG all skip NULL gaps.
